scenes.title: The decision frame
scenes.lede: Every sequence on three measured axes. Travel toward the host centroid is the horizontal; how much re-spelling it took is the depth; what the model actually decided is the height.

x.label: class axis  (0 = viral centroid, 1 = host centroid)

footnotes: Frozen classifier. Class axis length |mu_host - mu_viral| = 8.31 in embedding units.
All rewrite policies applied at a matched 50% synonymous edit budget on the same 40 viral parents. Every rewrite preserves the parent protein exactly.
The cone is one parent re-spelled at 5, 15, 30, 50, 80 and 100% of its mutable codons.

scenes.title: Five ways to write the same protein
scenes.lede: Every attack family lands its adversarials on the host side of the boundary. They do not all get there by travelling the same distance.

x.label: class axis  (0 = viral centroid, 1 = host centroid)

footnotes: Frozen classifier, 20 attacked parents. Depth is a family label, not a measured direction: this file records the class axis and the margin only.
P(viral) is the logistic of the recorded logit margin, so the boundary sits at 0.5 exactly where the margin crosses zero.
Only successful flips are stored, so every family reads 100% below the boundary by construction. This scene shows where flips land, not how often they succeed.

scenes.title: The walk across the boundary
scenes.lede: Each attack's edits applied in eighths. Height is how far through the edit set we are, so a thread rising while it crosses zero is a sequence being talked out of its own class.

z.label: fraction of the attack's edits applied

footnotes: Frozen classifier, 14 attacked parents, edits applied in the order the attack chose them. The boundary is the x = 0 wall.
Depth is the first principal component of the attack displacements with the decision direction projected out; it captures 21% of the off-axis variance.
The cone and the parents sit at zero edits applied, on the floor of the box.

scenes.title: Delete a direction, see what breaks
scenes.lede: Each row is one feature of the representation, not one sequence. Erase the subspace that carries it and re-score: the orange mark is what the screen scores afterwards, the grey mark is a random subspace of the same rank. The gap between them is the whole claim, and a short gap means the feature was not what the screen was using.
footnotes: Frozen classifier, 680 held-out sequences, 768-dimensional representation. Each row is a feature, so n is the number of features probed rather than a sample size.
The control erases a random subspace of the same rank, drawn with its 95% interval, so a feature only counts as load-bearing if erasing it costs more than erasing nothing in particular.
Erasing the class label itself, rank 12, lands at 0.559. That is the floor a feature has to reach before it can be called the thing the screen was using.

Hover carries how well a linear probe read each feature off the untouched representation. A feature can be almost perfectly readable and still cost nothing to erase, which is the point: readable is not the same as used.

scenes.title: Does the geometry survive a different encoder?
scenes.lede: Each mark is one CodonBERT layer, matched against its most similar layer in a second encoder family trained on raw nucleotides. Height is that similarity. Only pairs that clear a permutation null are eligible, and a row shows a mark at a layer only where one did.
footnotes: 160 sequences, mean-pooled. Mean pooling is what is plotted because it is the only pooling with trustworthy cells across all three model sizes.

A cell counts as trustworthy only if its CKA clears a permutation null. 52 of 507 layer pairs cleared it; the best one per CodonBERT layer is drawn, which is 39 marks. Cells that did not clear are left out rather than drawn faint.
Height is the best trustworthy match for that CodonBERT layer against any layer of the other encoder, so it is an upper bound on the correspondence at that depth.
Similarity of representations is not the same as agreement about the decision. Two encoders can align here and still differ on which features they act on.

scenes.title: Frozen, then hardened
scenes.lede: The same sequences scored by the frozen classifier and by the best hardened checkpoint. Play the move and every mark travels from where the frozen model put it to where the hardened one does, with faint ghosts left at both ends. Depth does not move: each sequence keeps its own frozen depth throughout, so everything you see travel is the class axis and the decision.

x.label: class axis  (measured in each model's own frame)

y.label: leading synonymous direction  (frozen frame, held fixed)

series.label: Adversarial, replayed at the hardened model, frozen
Adversarial, replayed at the hardened model, hardened
Adversarial, re-aimed at the hardened model

footnotes: Hardened checkpoint: three rounds of full fine-tuning on the adversarial pool, selected as the one that also lowers the adaptive attack rate.

Each model defines its own class axis from its own viral and host centroids, so x is a fraction of that model's centroid separation, not a shared embedding coordinate: the axis grows from 8.31 to 22.60 embedding units under hardening.

Depth is the frozen model's leading synonymous direction and is held at that value in both states. It was never recomputed for the hardened checkpoint, so it is carried along rather than re-measured, and no part of the move you see is depth.
The re-aimed adversarials have no frozen counterpart and so no frozen depth. They are drawn at depth 0 and fade in as the move completes.
The re-aimed attacker is a light re-run of the usage transplant against the hardened model at four edit fractions, not a full search. It is a floor on what an adaptive attacker gets, not a ceiling.
